QF.id: AIFM CII Fund Performance and Benchmarking_3

question.text: In the context of a Category I/II AIF, the 'J-curve' refers to:

answer.text: The convex shape of a zero-coupon bond's price-yield curve used in Cat II debt funds.
The inverse relationship between fund size and fee load.
The shape of the hurdle-rate catch-up distribution to the GP.
The typical pattern where the fund's cumulative cash flow (and IRR) is negative in the early vintage years and turns positive in maturity years as exits are realised.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Chapter 7.3.3, the J-curve describes the cash-flow profile of a closed-ended PE/VC fund: negative cumulative cash flow in the investment period (Y0-Y3 or so) because committed capital is being drawn and fees are being charged while exits haven't happened, followed by positive cash flow as investments are harvested in Y4-Y8. Plotted, this traces a letter 'J'. The Trap: A is a bond-pricing concept (XXI-A/XV); C is the distribution waterfall catch-up; D is a fee-structure observation — none describes the J-curve. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-B Cat III exam does NOT feature J-curve because Cat III funds typically redeem continuously. XIX-A distributors must explain J-curve to LPs so they don't panic in Y2 when IRR is deeply negative. Manager's Pro-Tip: When onboarding a first-time LP, set an explicit J-curve expectation in the PPM and quarterly report: 'Net IRR likely negative through Y3, crossing zero by Y4-Y5.' This pre-empts complaint calls at Q8 reporting.
